title: Chat — Service Health
description:
Triage surface: an alert fires, you open this, you read down until you know which layer broke. Row 1 is what users experience and names the service and the endpoint; row 2 is whether the processes are healthy; row 3 is the dependency client view.

Core path: message-gatekeeper, broadcast-worker, message-worker, roomlist-worker, notification-worker.

Server-side NATS, MongoDB and Cassandra health belongs to the teams that run them. Everything here is the client side.

list.name: datasource
list.label: Site
list.description: Each site runs its own Prometheus, so choosing the datasource chooses the site. There is deliberately no site variable.

list.name: namespace
list.label: Namespace
list.description: All means every namespace this variable lists, not every namespace in the cluster: no allValue is set, so Grafana builds the union of the options. With a literal .* the availability tiles counted unavailable replicas in kube-system and every other team's namespace.

list.name: name
list.label: Name filter
list.description: Substring matched against the container name, for the resource table and the two container charts in row 2. Those come from cAdvisor, which sees every container in the namespace including datastores, exporters and web UIs. Type nextgen to keep only nextgen-* containers; leave empty for all.

list.name: service
list.label: Service
list.description: Filters the application metrics. Its values come from a metric only our Go services emit, so it can never list a datastore or an exporter. The container panels in row 2 use the Name filter instead, because cAdvisor does not know a container's service_name.

panels.title: Core path unhealthy
panels.description:
Unavailable replicas on the five services a message must pass through: message-gatekeeper, broadcast-worker, message-worker, roomlist-worker, notification-worker. Matched as a substring, so a deployment-name prefix does not hide them.

NO DATA means kube-state-metrics is not being scraped here, not that everything is up -- the tile beside it will be empty for the same reason.

panels.title: All deployments unhealthy
panels.description: Unavailable replicas across every deployment, with no allowlist, so a service nobody has classified is still counted. The same number as the tile on the left means the problem is on the send path.

panels.title: API error rate
panels.description:
Failed calls over all calls, HTTP and NATS request/reply together. HTTP counts 5xx only: a 4xx is the service correctly refusing. NATS counts any call carrying error.type, which the convention omits on success.

This tile says how much, never who -- the two tables in row 1 name the route and the method.

targets.expr: 100 * ((sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", service_name=~"${service:regex}",http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[$__rate_interval])) or vector(0)) + (sum(rate(rpc_server_call_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", service_name=~"${service:regex}",error_type!=""}[$__rate_interval])) or vector(0))) / ((sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", service_name=~"${service:regex}"}[$__rate_interval])) or vector(0)) + (sum(rate(rpc_server_call_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", service_name=~"${service:regex}"}[$__rate_interval])) or vector(0)))

panels.title: Circuit breakers open
panels.description:
Breakers currently open or half-open. Four exist today: subscription and roommeta in message-gatekeeper, roommeta in broadcast-worker, atrestdek in message-worker and history-service. Each opens after MONGO_BREAKER_FAILS (default 5) consecutive qualifying failures and retries after MONGO_BREAKER_COOLDOWN (default 10s). A missing document is not a failure; a timeout is.

The gauge is written only on a transition, so a breaker that has never tripped since the process started has no series at all. An empty tile is the healthy state.

panels.title: Request rate by service
panels.description: Traffic, the golden signal an error-only dashboard leaves out. A drop is an outage upstream of these services, and while it lasts the error rate falls with it because nothing is arriving to fail.

panels.title: HTTP errors by service
panels.description: Broken out per service and status class, because the class alone cannot be acted on. 5xx is the service failing; 4xx is it refusing, and a 4xx spike during an auth incident is the symptom rather than the fault. The routes table below names the endpoint.

panels.title: NATS RPC errors by service and type
panels.description: error.type is absent on success, so every series here is a failure. unavailable and internal are the service breaking; unauthenticated, forbidden, not_found, conflict and bad_request are it working and saying no -- a rise in those is usually a client or a token, not an outage.

panels.title: HTTP latency by service
panels.description:
Solid is p95, dashed is p99, one pair per service. The gap between them is the diagnosis: p95 flat with p99 rising is a tail problem -- a retry, a GC pause, one bad pod, a cold path -- while both rising together is systemic.

p95 leads because it is the one that survives this fleet's traffic. A percentile needs samples above it to mean anything: p95 wants roughly 200 per window and p99 roughly 1000, so below about 3 requests per second p99 is a single slow call rather than a measurement. The req/s column in the table below says which you are looking at.

Both are interpolated inside a bucket, and every latency family in the repo shares one set of boundaries whose relative width is 100 to 150 percent. Read movement, not absolute values. The top boundary is 10s, so a line pinned there means at least 10s.

panels.title: NATS RPC latency by service
panels.description:
Solid p95, dashed p99, same reading as the HTTP panel beside it. Both share o11y's bucket boundaries on purpose, so the two panels are measured with the same ruler.

A service sitting at exactly 10s is not slow, it is timing out: the router's REQUEST_TIMEOUT defaults to 10s and the top histogram boundary is also 10s, so a timed-out call lands in the overflow bucket and the quantile reports the last finite boundary. Which of the two it is shows in the errors panel -- a router timeout is recorded as unavailable, and pkg/oidc's own 10s HTTP timeout surfaces as unauthenticated instead.

panels.title: HTTP routes
panels.description:
One row per route and service. Paths are templated by the gin middleware, so an id in the URL never becomes its own row. Sorted by error rate.

It opens sorted by traffic rather than by error rate, because error % is a division and is blank for a route with no calls in the window: sorting on a mostly empty column looks random. Click the error % header to rank by failure instead.

The latency column is p95, not p99. Sliced per route the sample count is small, and p99 over a handful of calls is the slowest one of them rather than a measurement. Read it beside req/s: a p95 on a route doing 0.02 requests per second is still barely evidence.

targets.expr: sum by (endpoint) (label_join(100 * sum by (service_name, http_route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", service_name=~"${service:regex}",http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (service_name, http_route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", service_name=~"${service:regex}"}[$__rate_interval])), "endpoint", " | ", "service_name", "http_route"))

sum by (endpoint) (label_join(histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, service_name, http_route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", service_name=~"${service:regex}"}[$__rate_interval]))), "endpoint", " | ", "service_name", "http_route"))

panels.title: NATS RPC methods
panels.description:
One row per service and rpc.method, sorted by error rate.

rpc.method is a curated enum mapped from the subject and it only covers room-service, history-service and the teams routes. Every call to user-service, search-service and media-service records unknown, so those rows are a whole service's request surface collapsed into one -- which is why the table groups by service too, otherwise three services would share a single row.

The router already computes a per-route wildcard pattern when the handler registers. Exporting it as a second label would make this one row per API; that is a change in pkg/natsmetrics.

targets.expr: sum by (endpoint) (label_join(100 * sum by (service_name, rpc_method) (rate(rpc_server_call_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", service_name=~"${service:regex}",error_type!=""}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (service_name, rpc_method) (rate(rpc_server_call_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", service_name=~"${service:regex}"}[$__rate_interval])), "endpoint", " | ", "service_name", "rpc_method"))

sum by (endpoint) (label_join(histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, service_name, rpc_method) (rate(rpc_server_call_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", service_name=~"${service:regex}"}[$__rate_interval]))), "endpoint", " | ", "service_name", "rpc_method"))

panels.title: Service resources
panels.description:
One row per container, from cAdvisor and kube-state. This is the ranked view: every column sorts, so click the one you are chasing. It opens sorted by restarts because that is the only column where any non-zero value is always a finding -- 80% CPU can be normal, three restarts never is.

Use the Name filter variable to cut it down; typing nextgen selects every nextgen-* container and drops the datastores, exporters and web UIs that share the namespace.

A blank in a % of limit column reads "no limit": either the container declares none, or kube-state-metrics is not scraped here. The absolute CPU and memory columns come from cAdvisor alone and are populated either way.

Restarts are counted inside the selected range. A pod that was replaced took its counter with it, so a crash followed by a reschedule is undercounted; the deploy markers cover that case.

targets.expr: 100 * sum by (container) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", container=~".*$name.*", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", container=~".*$name.*", container!="", container!="POD",resource="cpu"})

100 * sum by (container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", container=~".*$name.*", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", container=~".*$name.*", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval]))

100 * sum by (container) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", container=~".*$name.*", container!="", container!="POD"}) / sum by (container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", container=~".*$name.*", container!="", container!="POD",resource="memory"})

panels.title: CPU headroom: closest 10 to their limit
panels.description:
Cores used as a share of the container's CPU limit, for the ten containers running nearest their ceiling. This answers who is close to the edge, which the absolute core count cannot: half a core is a lot on a 0.5-core limit and nothing on four.

A container with no CPU limit cannot appear here -- there is no ceiling to be near. The table above carries its absolute usage, and its % of limit column reads "no limit", which for a production service is itself worth fixing: without a limit there is no throttling to protect the node and no number to derive GOMAXPROCS from.

targets.expr: topk(10, 100 * sum by (container) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", container=~".*$name.*", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", container=~".*$name.*", container!="", container!="POD",resource="cpu"}))

panels.title: Memory headroom: closest 10 to their limit
panels.description:
Working set as a share of the container's memory limit, for the ten closest to it. Working set is the number the kubelet uses for OOM kills and eviction, so this line reaching 100 is the kill.

A line that only ever climbs is the shape that ends in an OOM kill even while it is still well under the limit -- the slope matters as much as the level. Containers with no memory limit are absent for the same reason as the CPU panel.

targets.expr: topk(10, 100 * sum by (container) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", container=~".*$name.*", container!="", container!="POD"}) / sum by (container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", container=~".*$name.*", container!="", container!="POD",resource="memory"}))

panels.title: Go runtime configuration
panels.description:
Keyed by service_name from the OTel resource, a different label space from the container table above -- the bot- and teams- deployments run the same binary under a different service_name than their container name, so the two cannot be joined automatically. Compare by eye.

GOMAXPROCS well above the container's CPU limit is the most common cause of throttling: the scheduler opens that many Ps against a fraction of a core. GOMEMLIMIT is only published when it is actually set, so a blank means the runtime never feels the container's memory ceiling and will grow until the kernel intervenes -- blank is the finding, not missing data.

panels.title: Goroutines: highest 10 services
panels.description: Read the slope, not the value. Twenty thousand goroutines on a fan-out worker under load is normal; two hundred that become two thousand and never come back down after a deploy marker is a leak in a handler that stopped returning. A count that rises and falls with the request rate is working correctly.

panels.title: Datastore operations
panels.description: Client-side operation rate. This is what our processes asked for, not what the servers did -- the MongoDB, Cassandra and Valkey teams own the server view. Operation names carry no database or collection label, so traces are the only way further down.

panels.title: Datastore error ratio
panels.description: Share of client operations that returned an error, per datastore and service. error_type exists only on failures, so the numerator selects it and the denominator does not.

targets.expr: 100 * sum by (db_system_name, service_name) (rate(db_client_operation_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", service_name=~"${service:regex}",error_type!=""}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (db_system_name, service_name) (rate(db_client_operation_duration_seconds_count{namespace=~"${namespace:regex}", service_name=~"${service:regex}"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Datastore p99 latency
panels.description:
Client-observed p99, which includes the network and any driver retry. The gap between this and the server team's own latency panel is the round trip plus the retry, and that gap is the part we own.

Deliberately coarse: this family carries a bucket per service, operation and server address, and a full-resolution query over a long range trips Prometheus's sample limit. The step is pinned to one minute and the panel to 100 points. If it still fails, shorten the range -- the durable fix is a recording rule.

panels.title: Connection pool queue depth
panels.description: Requests waiting for a pooled connection. A flat zero is the healthy state and the expected reading -- the panel earns its place on the day it is not zero, because the datastore can be perfectly healthy while our side runs out of connections, and no server-side dashboard shows that.

panels.title: Connection pool checkout timeouts
panels.description: Checkouts that gave up waiting. Flat zero is healthy. Any sustained rate means requests are failing for want of a connection rather than anything the datastore did, and that pool sizing is the constraint.

panels.title: JetStream consumer loops
panels.description:
One row per service and durable, sorted so anything DOWN is at the top. A timeline of twenty green lanes is noise; what an operator needs is whether any lane is down and which.

The loop does not restart itself: it returns on a terminal error and stays gone until the process does, so DOWN here is permanent until someone restarts the pod. A liveness probe cannot see it -- the process is healthy, it is simply no longer consuming.

panels.title: NATS client connections
panels.description:
One row per service, sorted so a disconnected service is at the top. The underlying metric counts live connections rather than reporting a boolean, so it is clamped to one: the question here is connected or not.

A service that has lost its broker connection still answers its health probe and still serves HTTP. Its NATS publishes are the part that silently stops working.

panels.title: Circuit breakers
panels.description:
One row per service and breaker, sorted so open breakers are at the top. Four breakers exist: subscription and roommeta in message-gatekeeper, roommeta in broadcast-worker, atrestdek in message-worker and history-service.

A breaker publishes its state only when it transitions, so one that has never tripped since its process started has no row at all. An empty table is the healthy state, not missing instrumentation.
